post.yt_title: "Spare the Rod, Spoil the Child" Isn't in the Bible #shorts
post.yt_desc:
The Bible never says "spare the rod, spoil the child." That famous wording comes from the English poet Samuel Butler, in his satirical poem Hudibras (1660s).

The closest verse is in Proverbs, the Bible's book of wise sayings: "He who spares his rod hates his son, But he who loves him disciplines him promptly" (Proverbs 13:24 NKJV). Its point is love that cares enough to correct, not anger. Paul adds a balance for parents: "And you, fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath…" (Ephesians 6:4 NKJV).

And Jesus? When His disciples tried to turn children away, He was greatly displeased: "Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14 NKJV). Then He took them in His arms and blessed them.

📖 Read it yourself: Proverbs 13:24 · Ephesians 6:4 · Mark 10:13-16 (NKJV)

post.notes:
- 'Spare the rod and spoil the child' wording: Samuel Butler, Hudibras (Part II, 1664; Part I 1663): 'Love is a boy by poets styl'd, Then spare the rod, and spoil the child.' Similar older proverbs exist (e.g. Langland's Piers Plowman, 14th c.), so the script says 'the famous wording comes from', not 'invented'.
- Proverbs 13:24 NKJV verified (bible.com v114 search match 'disciplines him promptly'): "He who spares his rod hates his son, But he who loves him disciplines him promptly." Proverbs = Bible's wisdom book of sayings.
- Ephesians 6:4 NKJV: "And you, fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath, but bring them up in the training and admonition of the Lord." First clause quoted with …
- Mark 10:13-16: disciples rebuked those bringing children; v14 NKJV "But when Jesus saw it, He was greatly displeased and said to them, 'Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of God.'" v16 "And He took them up in His arms, laid His hands on them, and blessed them." (summarised, not quoted).
- No position on spanking taken; Christians differ on how to apply Proverbs' 'rod'.
